college_prep.title: College Prep
college_prep.tagline: Know what to do, and when to do it.
college_prep.intro: You do not need connections or insider knowledge to apply well. You need a checklist and a calendar. Here is both.

tasks: Take the PSAT/NMSQT (opens National Merit + practice)
Meet your school counselor; ask to be flagged for fee waivers
Start a simple list of colleges that interest you
Register for the SAT or ACT (fee waivers available for eligible students)
Visit campuses virtually or in person
Ask two teachers who know you well for recommendation letters
Build your college list: 2-3 reach, 3-4 target, 2-3 safety
Create your Common App and/or Coalition App account
Submit FAFSA on October 1 (as early as possible)
Submit Early Action / Early Decision apps (Nov 1 or Nov 15)
Request official transcripts and test scores
Submit Regular Decision apps (usually Jan 1 - Jan 15)
Complete the CSS Profile where required
Compare financial aid award letters (not just sticker price)
Commit by May 1 and submit your enrollment deposit (waivers exist)

financial_aid.title: Financial Aid
financial_aid.tagline: The sticker price is almost never what you pay.
financial_aid.intro: Financial aid is money for college you usually do not pay back - grants, scholarships, and work-study. Filing the FAFSA is the single most important thing you can do. It is free and it takes most families under an hour.

glossary.definition: Free Application for Federal Student Aid. The form that unlocks federal grants, loans, work-study, and most state and school aid. File every year.
An additional aid form (~$25, waivable) required by about 200 mostly-private colleges to award their own institutional grants.
Student Aid Index. A number from your FAFSA that colleges use to estimate what your family can contribute. Can be as low as -1500.
Federal grant of up to ~$7,400/year for students with high financial need. Does not need to be repaid.
Aid awarded because of your financial situation.
Aid awarded for grades, test scores, talent, or other achievements, regardless of need.
A college promises to cover 100% of your demonstrated need with aid (often no loans). About 70 colleges do this.
Total cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships. The number that actually matters when comparing colleges.
A part-time campus job funded by federal aid, with hours that flex around your classes.

steps: Create your FSA ID at studentaid.gov (both you and a parent need one).
Gather tax returns, W-2s, and records of untaxed income.
File the FAFSA as soon as it opens (Oct 1 / Dec 1 depending on year). Earlier = more aid available.
List every college you might apply to on the FAFSA - it costs nothing.
Check each college's site for a CSS Profile requirement and its own aid deadline.
Run each college's Net Price Calculator for a personalized estimate before you apply.
When awards arrive, compare net price, not sticker price. Appeal if your situation changed.

scholarships.title: Scholarships
scholarships.tagline: Free money, and there is a lot of it aimed at students like you.
scholarships.intro: Many scholarships specifically prioritize first-generation, low-income, and underrepresented students. Apply to a mix of large national programs and small local ones - local scholarships have far less competition.
tips: Start with local: your high school counselor's list, community foundations, employers, faith and cultural organizations.
Never pay to apply for or search for a scholarship. Legitimate scholarships are free.
Reuse your essays. Most prompts are variations on 'tell us about yourself' and 'why does this matter to you'.
Apply to small awards ($250-$1,000) - they add up and have low applicant counts.
Track deadlines in the same calendar as your college applications.
